proof:
# Exact coordinate-face support of the zero-diagonal geometric-mean image

For d>=1 let D_d be the compact convex downward set of row geometric means of nonnegative (d+1)-square column-stochastic zero-diagonal matrices. Write h_d(c)=max_(v in D_d) c dot v for c>=0.

Fix 2<=k<=d+1, r=(k-1)/d, and c_1,...,c_k>=0. Then

    h_d(c_1,...,c_k,0,...,0)
       =h_(k-1)(c_1^(1/r),...,c_k^(1/r))^r.             (1)

This is an exact support formula, including zero weights. It is not itself a capacity-containment theorem for general stochastic matrices.

Proof. In a maximizing matrix Y, transfer all mass in rows beyond k to one of the first k rows in the same column, avoiding its diagonal. Such a recipient exists because k>=2. This can only increase the objective. Thus the first k columns form a k-square zero-diagonal column-stochastic matrix Z on the active rows. Put

    a_i=(product_(j<=k,j!=i) Z_ij)^(1/(k-1)).

There are L=d-k+1 remaining columns. Denote their entries on the active rows by s_i,l, so each column is a probability vector. The objective is

    sum_i c_i a_i^r product_(l=1)^L s_i,l^(1/d).

If L=0, equation (1) is immediate. Otherwise generalized Hölder with exponents summing to one gives

    sum_i c_i a_i^r product_l s_i,l^(1/d)
       <=(sum_i c_i^(1/r) a_i)^r,

because every sum_i s_i,l is one. For completeness this version of Hölder follows from weighted AM-GM after normalizing each nonnegative sequence by its sum; summing the resulting product bound gives at most one. It remains valid when some entries vanish by continuity.

Equality is achieved for fixed Z by taking every remaining column equal to

    s_i,l = c_i^(1/r) a_i / sum_j c_j^(1/r) a_j.

If the denominator vanishes, both sides are zero and any probability columns suffice. Maximizing over Z is therefore exactly the support function on the right of (1). The compact matrix domains ensure these maxima are attained. This proves the formula.

In particular

    h_3(c_1,c_2,c_3,0)=h_2(c_1^(3/2),c_2^(3/2),c_3^(3/2))^(2/3).

Taking k=2 and using D_1=[0,1]^2 gives h_d(c_1,c_2,0,...,0)=(c_1^d+c_2^d)^(1/d), agreeing with the exact two-coordinate face proved in the companion tetrahedral/capacity note. For d=1 this is the support of the square, as required.

The right-hand formula concerns a support function, not coordinatewise powers of D_(k-1). Replacing it by a coordinatewise-power containment would be an additional unproved claim and is not used.
